source.title: Characterizing Implicit Bias in Terms of Optimization Geometry
source.authors: Suriya Gunasekar; J. Lee; Daniel Soudry; N. Srebro

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some equations and symbols are garbled by text extraction, but the relevant prose and theorem statements are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper argues that optimization geometry shapes implicit bias, but tests linear models on synthetic or unspecified separable data and explicitly cautions that further work is needed to extend the results to nonlinear neural networks. Its results refine the scope of optimizer and initialization effects, rather than directly testing the catalog's neural-network generalization versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's own results concern which solutions optimization methods reach in underdetermined linear regression and separable linear classification. It does not measure train–test error or test generalization on natural data. The deep-network generalization claims in the introduction and cited Wilson et al. results are prior work, not this paper's results. Record the paper's own optimization-geometry results under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study characterizes optimization limits in linear regression and separable linear classification. It reports no held-out performance, width comparison, sharpness–gap correlation, or other outcome named by V1–V8. Its AdaGrad result concerns initialization-dependent solution directions, not V4's optimizer generalization comparison. Neural-network generalization findings are cited prior work.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: optimization geometry and loss determine implicit bias in the studied linear models. Mirror descent has a conditional minimum-divergence characterization; steepest descent with exponential loss has a maximum-margin characterization under stated conditions; AdaGrad can retain initialization and step-size dependence. The matrix-factorization result establishes conditional first-order stationarity, rather than global nuclear-norm optimality. Extension to nonlinear neural networks remains future work.
record.recipe_differences: Theoretical and empirical analysis of linear models and optimization geometry; it does not use the natural-data neural-network training recipes in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: For finite-root losses, the selected solution can depend on primal momentum or finite step sizes for natural gradient and general steepest descent. For strictly monotone losses, steepest descent's maximum-margin characterization holds under a step-size bound; AdaGrad retains dependence on initialization and step size.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 1 characterizes mirror descent's limit as the feasible solution minimizing Bregman divergence to initialization, conditional on convergence to zero loss. Extensions cover dual momentum and instancewise stochastic gradients under stated conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For realizable linear objectives with unique-finite-root losses, mirror descent has a conditional minimum-divergence implicit bias.

fits_no_version.finding: Examples 2–4 and Figure 1 show that primal momentum changes mirror descent's selected solution, finite step sizes change natural gradient descent's solution, and general-norm steepest descent can fail to select the minimum-norm solution even in the infinitesimal-step limit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Minimum-potential or minimum-norm characterizations of linear regression optimization depend on the algorithm, momentum formulation, and step-size regime.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 5 establishes convergence of normalized margins to the norm-specific maximum margin for separable linear classification with exponential loss and the stated step-size bound; direction convergence follows when the maximum-margin solution is unique.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Norm-based steepest descent on separable exponential-loss linear classification asymptotically maximizes the corresponding margin under stated conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 6 establishes bounded accumulated AdaGrad coordinate statistics under stated conditions; Section 3.3 concludes that initialization and step size can retain influence on the limiting direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: AdaGrad's implicit bias on separable exponential-loss linear classification can depend on initialization and step size.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 7 conditionally identifies the limiting factor direction with a scaled first-order stationary point of a factorized margin problem. Global nuclear-norm margin optimality is a stronger result left for future work.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under loss and direction-convergence assumptions, gradient descent on factorized linear predictors approaches a stationary direction of a factorized margin problem.

record.problems: The results are for linear models and do not directly establish effects on neural-network generalization. Several claims are asymptotic or conditional on convergence, separability, and bounded step sizes. Some illustrative comparisons are described through figures; no train–test error outcomes are reported.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying rows: cited deep-network generalization findings are prior work, and this paper's own results measure optimization limits in linear models rather than the behaviors in the claim versions.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label held-out accuracy, and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as network width increases beyond the width required to fit training data.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classification performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers' held-out performance under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Dropout effects on test error, including training-set size, underfitting, and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness correlations with generalization gaps and comparisons with other measures.
Test-accuracy effects of removing highly memorized versus random training examples.

record.verdict_notes: The empty row set is appropriate. The reader's tests/T5 classification should be corrected: these related optimization results neither test nor specifically refute any supplied version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test memorization of random labels or natural-label generalization.
Does not vary network width or measure test error across widths.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected networks.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers' held-out performance; the AdaGrad analysis is on linear separable classification and studies limit-direction dependence.
Does not vary batch size or measure generalization gaps.
Does not measure sharpness or correlate it with a train–test gap.
Does not remove memorized examples or measure the resulting test accuracy.
